newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Food aid vital for Albania's poorest.
newsitem.headline: Food aid vital for Albania's poorest.

text.p: Albania's poor desperately need food as they wait for a multinational force to protect relief shipments, the U.N. World Food Programme said on Monday.

Their basic food costs have shot up since the country slid into anarchy in February, their social security payments have stopped and state food supplies are not reaching orphanages or homes for the handicapped and elderly, WFP spokeswoman Laura Boldrini told Reuters.

"There is no starvation in Albania, but there is a need for food assistance, especially for institutions such as orphanages and homes for the elderly and handicapped, and destitute families," she said.
"Furthermore, many families need assistance because they cannot afford to buy food which is more expensive."
An armed insurrection has claimed nearly 300 lives in Europe's poorest country after the failure of get-rich-quick investment schemes that wiped out many small savers.
The WFP, the world's largest international food aid organisation, will rely on the multinational mission to escort it in unsafe areas, Bordini said.
"We will not distribute food unescorted to places that are not secure," she said.

The WFP's first shipment of more than 400 tonnes of wheat flour, beans and vegetable oil was expected in the western port of Durres on Tuesday, coinciding with the arrival of troops from an Italian-led, 6,000-strong force.
The U.N.-backed force also includes soldiers from France, Spain, Greece, Turkey, Austria, Denmark and Romania.
Some 150,000 families among Albania's 3.4 million people need food aid, according to the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs. Beggars are a common sight in Albania.
Amid signs that the government was making progress to restore order, the Albanian military staged a ceremony in Durres to show that it had regrouped a 400-strong infantry battalion.
The armed forces disintegrated as many soldiers deserted their posts at the height of the uprising.
"The principal aim was to boost the morale of the soldiers," Defence Minister Shaqir Vukaj told reporters at the military compound after the ceremony.
"We are working to reorganise the army in the whole of Albania and we hope we will succeed."
Major General Ali Koceku, the battalion commander, said: "The main thing is that this is the first unit that has been reorganised in the whole Albanian army."

He added: "The message that this unit brings is very important for all of Albania and all of the army. It's a message of peace. It's a message for the future, for the reorganisation of the Albanian army."
Albanian Foreign Minister Arjan Starova left for Rome where he was expected to sign an agreement assigning troops from each member state to key locations across the country.

Finance Minister Arben Malaj, who on Sunday met representatives of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, visited London for talks with European Reconstruction and Development officials to discuss the reconstruction.

Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino said in an interview with Austrian daily Die Presse that the state had regained authority over much of the southern region, where rebel committees have been in charge for more than a month.
"The situation has improved, local authorities have the situation under control. Many (rebel) committees have been dissolved and the authorities taken charge," he said.
Fino's Socialists joined President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party in an all-party emergency government a month ago.

In fresh violence on Sunday, gunmen killed a bus conductor in the village of Buz in southern Albania after he refused to give them money, witnesses said. An 18-year-old boy died in nearby Kaludh after a grenade he was playing with blew up.
